extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and teachers studying literature (particularly William Golding's Lord of the Flies) and writers interested in craft examples from an allegorical novel
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting craft and evaluative principles illustrated by Lord of the Flies — e.g., thematic focus, use of symbolism, characterisation, tone, and editorial shaping — to inform writing or literary analysis of allegorical/philosophical fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central themes (morality, leadership, civility vs chaos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel's themes include morality, leadership, and the tension between civility and chaos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an explicit thematic core that examines human nature and social order; frame the narrative to explore conflicts (e.g., civilisation vs savagery, individual vs group) so the story can operate allegorically while still engaging readers. The page repeatedly foregrounds these themes as the novel's major concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre classification: allegorical and philosophical fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: As a tale of adventure and survival, Lord of the Flies fits the genre of allegorical fiction. It also questions human morality, making it a work of philosophical fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or evaluating allegory/philosophical fiction, expect the work to embody abstract ideas (human savagery, mob mentality, leadership dynamics) through plot and character; ensure the narrative prompts ethical or philosophical reflection rather than serving only as plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviation from simplistic allegory: fully developed realistic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Golding deviates from typical allegory in that both the protagonists and the antagonists are fully developed, realistic characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-dimensional personifications in allegory. Even when characters represent ideas, they should be believable and complex so the allegory gains psychological depth and emotional resonance. The page highlights this deviation as a key craft choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concrete symbolism (objects representing abstract concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some examples of symbolism in Lord of the Flies are the signal fire, Piggy's glasses, and the conch shell, which may be read as representing hope, reason, democracy, and unity, among other interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ tangible, recurring objects or motifs that can carry multiple symbolic readings. Make their function in the story concrete (e.g., the glasses literally start fires) so symbolism arises naturally from plot mechanics. The article lists specific objects and suggested readings as exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism of behaviour vs romanticised adventure (reaction against The Coral Island)
rubrics_metrics.description: Golding thought that The Coral Island was unrealistic and wrote a book about children on an island, children who behave in the way children really would behave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aiming for psychological/verisimilar fiction, prioritise believable behaviour over idealised or romanticised outcomes. Use contrast with prior genre conventions to justify tonal or moral choices; the page uses Golding's stated intent as a craft rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical/contextual setting (war/Cold War) to inform theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Golding, who experienced war firsthand... After the war ended and Golding returned to England, the world was dominated by the Cold War and the threat of nuclear annihilation, which led Golding to examine the nature of humanity and that went on to inspire Lord of the Flies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor allegorical concerns in an explicit historical or geopolitical context to deepen thematic stakes. Background events (war, political tension) can provide subtext that amplifies the novel's examination of violence, authority, and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial shaping and revision (cutting, focusing character arcs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor Charles Monteith worked with Golding on several major edits, including removing the entire first section that described an evacuation from nuclear war. The character of Simon also was heavily edited to remove an interaction with a mysterious figure who is implied to be a god.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant revision and selective cutting can strengthen thematic focus and tone. Editors may remove explicit exposition or scenes that dilute ambiguity (e.g., overt supernatural implications) to preserve interpretive complexity. The article uses specific editorial changes to illustrate this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title/allusion as thematic signal
rubrics_metrics.description: The title is a literal translation of Beelzebub, a biblical demon considered the god of pride and warfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose titles or allusive language that resonate symbolically with major themes (e.g., pride, warfare). Explicit intertextual references can prime readers for allegorical readings and deepen thematic layering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and register: bleakness fused with universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Lord of the Flies presents a view of humanity unimaginable before the horrors of Nazi Europe, and then plunges into speculations about mankind in the state of nature. Bleak and specific, but universal, fusing rage and grief, Lord of the Flies is both a novel of the 1950s, and for all time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance specificity (historical or situational detail) with a tone that aspires to universality so the story feels both grounded and widely applicable. Use emotional intensity (rage, grief) to convey moral seriousness without reducing complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate controversy and pedagogical suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Lord of the Flies was included on the American Library Association list of the 100 most frequently challenged books of 1990–1999, for its controversial stance on human nature and individual welfare versus the common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When works depict violence, cynical views of humanity, or challenge prevailing moral frameworks, expect debates about suitability for classroom or public audiences. Authors and educators should be prepared to justify thematic aims and contextualise difficult content.
